segments.speaker: John
segments.text: In a hypothetical course on Multimodal Learning and Reliable AI, today’s lecture is on “Mitigating Cross-Modal Hallucinations by Correcting Modality Misrouting in Omnimodal LLMs.” Recent work such as “Attention Reallocation” and “AVCD” reflects a broader trend toward inference-time ways to reduce hallucinations. This paper, from researchers affiliated with Zhejiang University and Ant Group, asks a more specific question: what if the model already has the right evidence, but fails to use it in its joint prediction? I see a hand. Yes, Noah?

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Hi Professor, does modality misrouting mean the model is paying attention to the wrong input?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That is close, though the paper defines it through a particular pattern: a joint audio-video answer is wrong, while the relevant audio-only or video-only branch can still answer correctly. The evidence has not vanished; it is underrepresented in the fused prediction. The authors measure this recovery pattern on cross-modal benchmarks and find it in a substantial share of errors, motivating a correction that uses the model’s own unimodal representations.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The method, called care, first asks a text-only question about which modality is needed to answer the prompt: audio, video, or both. Because this probe sees the question but not the sensory sample, it serves as a routing guide rather than an answer. If it uniquely selects audio or video, care compares that modality’s branch with the joint audio-video branch. If the probe does not select one modality, the ordinary joint prediction is left unchanged.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: So the method does not automatically trust whichever single-modality answer sounds more confident?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Exactly. Care also requires a conflict: the joint and selected unimodal branches must each have a clear prediction, and those predictions must differ. For example, a video of a cat might bias the joint model toward claiming it hears a meow, even when the audio contains duck calls. If the audio-only branch says “no,” and the question probe points to audio, the conflict gate allows a correction. Otherwise, the method makes no intervention.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: For a gate-positive case, care compares internal hidden states from the joint and selected unimodal branches. Their difference supplies a sample-specific residual direction. The method adds a scaled version of that difference to the joint representation, rather than substituting the unimodal answer. Think of it as using a counterfactual branch as a guide to adjust the model’s route, while keeping both sensory inputs available for the rest of the answer.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Can you clarify where that representation adjustment happens?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The intervention happens at the final prompt-token position during prefilling, in the final 3 language-decoder layers in the main experiments. The adjusted state then passes through later decoder layers, and generation continues on the audio-video path. The correction strength depends on the unimodal branch’s decision margin: more decisive predictions can receive stronger steering. The coefficients also decrease across the selected layers, so early layers get more adjustment than later ones.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: This design relies on three linked ideas: route using the question, intervene only when branch predictions conflict, and correct the joint representation without dropping either modality. Across the C-M-M benchmark, care raises accuracy from 70.5% to 85.9% for quen two point five omni seven B, and from 73% to 86.9% for mini C-P-M o two point six. On A-V-H-Bench, the corresponding results rise from 69.8% to 82.3%, and from 73.4% to 80.2%.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Does the method help both kinds of cross-modal errors, or mainly one direction?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The reported results cover both directions: visual evidence inducing a false audio perception, and audio evidence inducing a false visual perception. Gains are especially apparent on the Audio Dominance subset of C-M-M. The team also tests quen two point five omni three B, where accuracy rises from 76.9% to 82.5% on C-M-M and from 76.4% to 81% on A-V-H-Bench. That offers evidence across model scales, though still within a limited set of backbones.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: A useful ablation compares representation correction with simply taking the selected unimodal branch’s answer. Care performs better across the reported backbone-task combinations, with gains over direct selection reaching 10.82 percentage points. This supports the idea that the joint context remains valuable even when it has misrouted evidence. On Daily-Omni, broader audio-visual question-answering accuracy changes modestly, from 61.5% to 61.8% for one model and from 61% to 61.5% for the other, with variation across categories.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: How should we compare this with Attention Reallocation or AVCD?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: Those works also explore inference-time mitigation, but care’s distinctive emphasis is identifying a recoverable disagreement between a joint branch and a question-selected unimodal branch, then steering the joint representation. It is not a global reweighting rule or simply a contrastive output adjustment. That makes it a targeted response to modality misrouting. The comparison also suggests a broader research direction: diagnosing where useful evidence is lost inside a multimodal computation, then intervening selectively.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: There are important constraints. The method assumes a finite answer set, such as yes or no, so branch predictions and margins can be compared. It also assumes the relevant evidence is accessible in a unimodal branch and that the question-only probe selects a useful modality. Extra probe and counterfactual passes add inference cost, even though the paper reports lower serial-execution latency than M-A-D and notes that parallel branches could reduce latency further.

segments.speaker: Noah
segments.text: Could this approach work for open-ended questions where there is no fixed set of answers?

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: That remains an open question. Extending care to open-ended generation would require reliable ways to compare branch claims and identify meaningful conflicts without a predefined answer space. More broadly, the paper shifts attention from suppressing suspicious outputs toward recovering evidence the model already represents. Its benchmark results support that strategy for binary cross-modal tasks, while leaving broader tasks, more models, and deployment costs for future evaluation.

segments.speaker: John
segments.text: The central takeaway is simple: a multimodal model can possess the evidence it needs and still fail to route that evidence into its answer. Care offers a selective way to use a unimodal branch as a guide while retaining joint context. Whether this pattern generalizes beyond the tested settings will depend on better routing, wider evaluations, and practical control of inference cost. Thanks for listening.
